Keep the empty settings descriptor and empty dashboard-card list — the generic pump card already renders pairing status and Unpair. Replace TandemGlucoseSource's naive 60 s polling flow with an AsyncStream fed by the shared connection scheduler, because two independent pollers competing for a single-connection pump is worse on iOS than on Android.

needs_redesign.why: Not a limitation of watchOS BLE — watchOS does have CoreBluetooth — but of the pump: Tandem pumps accept exactly one BLE connection at a time, so a Watch that connects steals the connection from the iPhone. Compounding it, watchOS has no bluetooth-central background mode and no CBCentralManager state restoration, so a watch-side driver could not maintain a session anyway.
options: Watch is a pure consumer: iPhone owns the pump connection and pushes readings over WatchConnectivity, with complications and Smart Stack fed from the transferred data.
Watch as an alternate connection owner when the phone is out of range, with an explicit handoff.
Independent watchOS app with its own pump connection.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, unequivocally. Use WCSession updateApplicationContext for latest-value state (coalescing, survives being backgrounded) and transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo for complication-driving updates, with a defined budget-exhaustion fallback. Complications and Smart Stack widgets render from the last transferred snapshot with an explicit staleness age — never a stale number with no age. Option 2 should be explicitly ruled out in the PRD: connection stealing during a handoff race would leave both devices unable to read the pump.

needs_redesign.why: CoreBluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator, and the lead developer has a pump and a Mac but no iPhone. Without a substitute, essentially none of this subsystem is exercisable by the person writing it, and every change would queue behind the one maintainer with hardware.
options: A protocol-level transport abstraction with a scripted fake peripheral that replays captured pump traffic, driving the real state machine, auth, framing and parsers in the Simulator and on CI.
A macOS harness target that links the identical Swift driver package and talks to a real t:slim X2 over the Mac's own Bluetooth — CoreBluetooth is fully available on macOS.
Rely solely on the maintainer's iPhone.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Both 1 and 2, and treat them as first-class deliverables rather than test scaffolding. Define the driver's dependency on CoreBluetooth as a narrow protocol (scan, connect, discover, subscribe, write, notify, disconnect, state) so a FakeTransport can drive the entire stack in unit tests and a SimulatedPump can drive the whole app in the Simulator. The macOS bench is the higher-leverage item: it lets the lead developer validate real JPAKE pairing, real framing and real history paging against his own pump with no iPhone at all, leaving Daniel's hardware for iOS-specific behavior — background wakes, state restoration, Keychain-while-locked, watch delivery — which is exactly the set the Mac cannot cover. Caveat the bench honestly: the pump's single-connection limit means the Mac and the iPhone cannot both be paired-and-connected at once.

needs_redesign.capability: Security and dependency gates for this module
needs_redesign.why: The Android gates for this code are Semgrep --config p/kotlin,p/java,p/secrets, OSV-Scanner v2.3.3 over committed Gradle lockfiles, and a pinned bcprov-jdk18on 1.84. Semgrep's registry has no maintained Swift ruleset, so 'run Semgrep' is not portable; the requirement is the substance, not the tool name.
options: SAST: CodeQL with language: swift on a macOS runner (GitHub's supported Swift analysis) as the direct replacement for Semgrep p/kotlin+p/java.
Secrets: keep Semgrep --config p/secrets (language-agnostic regexes, works unchanged on Swift) and/or gitleaks — a true name-for-name carryover.

Dependencies: OSV-Scanner v2 already parses Package.resolved, so the same tool and the same osv-scanner.toml suppression discipline carry over verbatim once Package.resolved is committed and pinned to exact versions.
Lint/quality: SwiftLint plus swift build -warnings-as-errors as the rough analogue of detekt/ktlint; periphery for dead code.
Workflow supply chain: zizmor and the workflow-lint/workflow-security jobs are language-agnostic and carry over unchanged.
needs_redesign.recommendation: CodeQL(swift) + Semgrep p/secrets + OSV-Scanner on a committed, exact-pinned Package.resolved + SwiftLint, and state plainly in the PRD that CodeQL's Swift coverage is narrower than Semgrep's Kotlin rules — the compensating control is that this module's risk surface is memory-safe parsing and crypto, both of which are better covered by the ported vector tests and a differential test against the Kotlin EC-JPAKE than by any generic ruleset. Two Android-specific gates simply disappear: consumer ProGuard rules (no R8) and the instrumented-test requirement for Base64 (Foundation Base64 unit-tests on CI). Note that if the pure-Swift EC option is chosen there is no third-party crypto dependency left to scan at all, which is a meaningful supply-chain improvement over pinning BouncyCastle.

impossible.capability: BluetoothGatt.refresh() — clearing the cached GATT service database on every connect
impossible.why: There is no public or private CoreBluetooth API to invalidate the OS service cache, and no reflection escape hatch on iOS. iOS caches a bonded peripheral's service database and will not re-discover on its own. The Android driver calls refresh() on every STATE_CONNECTED specifically because a stale cache silently drops notifications — the exact failure mode iOS is also susceptible to.
impossible.closest_alternative: Rely on the standards-based mechanism: implement peripheral(_:didModifyServices:) and re-run discovery when the pump sends a GATT Service Changed indication (0x2A05). Handle characteristic references going invalid after any reconnect by re-discovering rather than caching CBCharacteristic objects across sessions. For a genuinely stale cache the only user-facing remedy is forgetting the device in iOS Settings, which iOS clears the cache on — so this becomes a documented troubleshooting step rather than an automatic recovery.

impossible.why: iOS exposes no API to enumerate, inspect or delete Bluetooth pairings. The user must do it manually in Settings → Bluetooth → Forget This Device. Three Android code paths depend on removeBond (status 0x05 before CONNECTED, status 0x08 with no prior successful session, and three zero-response connections) and none of them can be automated.
impossible.closest_alternative: Detect the same conditions with the same counters, then surface a specific, actionable recovery instruction instead of acting: clear app-side credentials, set AUTH_FAILED, and tell the user exactly which two things to do (forget the pump in iOS Settings, then put the pump into pairing mode and re-pair). Because the automatic remedy is gone, the Android restraint policy matters even more — do not trip this state on transient encryption failures once a successful session has occurred.

impossible.why: CoreBluetooth gives the central no control over connection interval, latency or supervision timeout. Only the peripheral may request parameters, via an L2CAP Connection Parameter Update Request, and iOS applies its own policy to what it accepts (Apple's accessory guidelines constrain acceptable intervals to multiples of 15 ms with a minimum of 15 ms). The Android code requests HIGH priority because the pump drops connections at slower intervals.
impossible.closest_alternative: None on the central side. The mitigating fact is that Tandem ships an official iOS t:connect app, so the pump firmware demonstrably negotiates workable parameters with iOS and requests them itself. Verify empirically on Daniel's hardware whether the session survives; if it does not, the only remaining lever is the connect → burst-read → disconnect cycle, which keeps each session short enough that interval-driven timeouts do not accumulate.

impossible.capability: requestMtu(185) and treating MTU negotiation failure as fatal
impossible.why: iOS negotiates the ATT MTU automatically at connection setup and exposes no request API. There is no MTU callback and therefore no MTU-failure branch to implement.
impossible.closest_alternative: Functionally a non-issue and arguably an improvement: iOS requests an ATT MTU of 185 automatically (matching REQUIRED_MTU exactly), and the driver chunks every write at 18 bytes regardless. Replace the fatal MTU gate with a readiness assertion on peripheral.maximumWriteValueLength(for: .withResponse) >= 20, logged for diagnostics, and delete the close-GATT-and-give-up path that MTU failure triggered on Android.

impossible.capability: A foreground service holding a permanent connection with a guaranteed 15 s poll cadence in the background
impossible.why: iOS has no foreground services and no user-visible persistent-work affordance that grants unbounded runtime. With the bluetooth-central background mode the connection object survives, but a suspended app cannot initiate a write; runtime is granted only when the peripheral generates an event, and this pump generates none unsolicited. BGAppRefreshTask (~30 s, system-scheduled, typically minutes to hours apart) and BGProcessingTask (charging/idle) cannot deliver a 15 s cadence. Battery-optimization exemptions and Samsung 'Sleeping apps' have no iOS analogue because the restriction is not a setting.
impossible.closest_alternative: Event-driven wakeups instead of timer-driven polling: disconnect after each read burst and leave an indefinite connect() outstanding so the next connection event wakes the app, plus BGProcessingTask for opportunistic history backfill. Accept and state plainly that background freshness is best-effort. The history log makes gaps recoverable, so the honest product promise is 'complete data with variable latency in the background, Android-equivalent cadence in the foreground', surfaced with an explicit data-age indicator rather than an implied-fresh number.

impossible.capability: Apple Watch connecting to the pump directly
impossible.why: The pump accepts exactly one BLE connection at a time, so a watch-side connection necessarily steals it from the iPhone; there is no shared-connection mode. Independently, watchOS provides neither the bluetooth-central background mode nor CBCentralManager state restoration, so a watch-side driver could not sustain or recover a session even if it were the sole owner. This is a device constraint compounded by a platform one, not an engineering gap.
impossible.closest_alternative: iPhone owns the pump connection exclusively; the Watch receives readings over WatchConnectivity (updateApplicationContext for latest state, transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo for complication updates) and renders complications and Smart Stack entries from the last transferred snapshot with a visible data age. watchOS also has no custom watch faces, so the Android watchface module's role is served by complications on Apple's own faces plus Smart Stack widgets — a narrower surface that should be scoped as such rather than promised as parity.

ios_requirements: A user must be able to discover a Tandem t:slim X2 or Tandem Mobi from the iPhone app by scanning for the pump's fdfb service while the pump is in pairing mode, seeing each discovered pump's name and signal strength, and being told plainly when nothing appears because the pump is not advertising, Bluetooth is off, or Bluetooth permission was denied.

A user must be able to complete first-time pairing by entering the pump's pairing code (6-digit from the t:slim X2 screen, or the 16-character code printed on a Mobi), with the app selecting the JPAKE or V1 handshake automatically from the code length and never asking the user which protocol their pump speaks.
The app must accept and complete an iOS Bluetooth pairing prompt as part of first connection, and must tell the user in advance that the prompt will appear and must be accepted for the pump to work.

After a successful pairing the app must reconnect to the same pump automatically, without the pump being put back into pairing mode and without the user re-entering the code, for as long as the pairing is intact.

The app must keep attempting to reconnect indefinitely while a pairing exists, only stopping when the user unpairs or when the app has positively determined the pairing is no longer valid — a medical monitoring app must never quietly give up on the pump.

When the app determines the pairing is genuinely broken, it must say so distinctly (not as an ordinary disconnect) and give the user the exact recovery steps, including forgetting the pump in iOS Settings, since the app cannot remove an iOS Bluetooth pairing itself.

The app must tolerate transient encryption and connection failures after at least one successful session without invalidating the pairing, so that sleep/wake and out-of-range events never strand a user without pump data.

The app must surface pump connection status to the user as distinct, actionable states: connected, connecting, authenticating, reconnecting, disconnected, pairing invalid, Bluetooth off, and Bluetooth permission denied.
While the app is in the foreground the user must see pump data refresh at Android-equivalent cadence, with insulin-on-board, basal rate and glucose visible within seconds of opening the app.

While the app is backgrounded the system must continue collecting pump data opportunistically whenever iOS grants it Bluetooth runtime, and must back-fill any gap from the pump's history log once a session is re-established, so that no delivered bolus, basal change or glucose reading is permanently lost to a background gap.

Every pump-derived value shown anywhere in the app or on the Watch must carry a visible data age, and values older than a configured threshold must be visually distinguished, because iOS cannot guarantee background refresh timing.
The app must resume history collection from where it left off across app termination and system relaunch, so that a killed process does not cause repeated re-reads or skipped records.

The app must read from the pump only. It must never issue a bolus, change a basal rate, alter a pump setting, or write to any pump control characteristic, and this must be enforced by the driver interface rather than by convention.

The app must reject any glucose value outside 20–500 mg/dL, any bolus above 25 U, and any basal rate above 15 U/hr from every parsing path, live and historical, before that value reaches storage, the dashboard, alerts, or any AI analysis.

The app must convert pump timestamps to the phone's current local time using the Tandem 2008 epoch and the pump's local-wall-clock semantics, producing timestamps identical to the Android app for the same pump bytes in any time zone.
The app must report only completed insulin deliveries as delivered insulin, never started, cancelled or errored ones.
The app must categorize each bolus (Control-IQ automatic, correction, food, food-and-correction, override, other) identically to the Android app for the same pump data.
The app must read pump battery level and reservoir volume on both t:slim X2 and Mobi, and must never issue the battery request variant that is known to terminate a t:slim X2 session.
The app must report the pump's model, serial number, firmware version and feature flags, and must continue to function with reduced detail when the pump does not return them.

An Apple Watch user must see current glucose with trend, insulin on board, basal rate and pump connection status, delivered from the iPhone, on a complication and in the Smart Stack, each with a visible data age and an explicit indication when the phone has not been reachable.

A maintainer must be able to run the complete pump protocol stack — framing, CRC, reassembly, both authentication handshakes, and every parser — as automated tests on a CI runner with no phone, no pump and no Bluetooth hardware.
A developer with a Mac and a pump but no iPhone must be able to exercise the real driver against the real pump from macOS, covering pairing, authentication, status reads and history paging.

A developer must be able to run the entire app in the iOS Simulator against a simulated pump that produces realistic protocol traffic, including pairing, reconnection, and failure cases such as bad pairing codes and dropped sessions.

The pump pairing code and derived pairing secret must be stored so they are readable when the device is locked but only after first unlock, must never leave the device, and must never sync to iCloud or appear in an encrypted backup restored to another device.

Diagnostic packet logs must be available to the user for troubleshooting, must never include glucose values, insulin doses, pump serial numbers or Bluetooth identifiers in system logs, and must not be persisted unencrypted.

The repository's CI must gate every change to the pump driver on: static security analysis of Swift source, secret scanning, known-vulnerability scanning of pinned Swift package dependencies, lint, and the full protocol test suite including the published safety-constant and pump-time vectors.
The project must document, and CI must verify, that the Swift EC-JPAKE implementation produces byte-identical handshake messages to the Android implementation for the same inputs.

The app must ship the required Bluetooth usage description and Bluetooth central background mode, and must degrade to a clear explanatory state rather than a crash or a blank screen if Bluetooth permission is denied or restricted.

risks.risk: iOS gives the central no control over connection interval. The Android driver explicitly requests a 7.5–15 ms interval because the pump drops connections at slower defaults; if the pump behaves the same way against iOS's ~30 ms default, sessions may drop before authentication completes and there is no API-level fix.
risks.mitigation: Test this first, before any other hardware work, on Daniel's iPhone against a real t:slim X2 — a bare connect + JPAKE + one status read is enough to answer it. The reassuring prior is that Tandem's own t:connect iOS app works, so the pump must request acceptable parameters itself. If sessions do drop, fall back to short connect → auth → burst-read → disconnect cycles so no session lives long enough to accumulate an interval-driven timeout.

risks.risk: Background data collection cannot match Android's 15 s cadence, because a poll-only peripheral generates no CoreBluetooth events and a suspended iOS app cannot initiate reads. If the PRD promises Android-equivalent background freshness, the product will not deliver it.
risks.mitigation: Architect around connection-event-driven wakeups plus history backfill rather than a background poll loop, state the honest promise in the PRD (complete data, variable background latency), and make data age visible everywhere so a stale number is never mistaken for a fresh one.

risks.risk: The EC-JPAKE core must be rewritten from BouncyCastle to Swift with no library that exposes the needed P-256 point arithmetic. A subtle error — a wrong encoding length, a mis-reduced ZKP hash, an unblinded scalar — produces a handshake that fails only against real pump firmware, which the lead developer cannot reach without hardware.
risks.mitigation: Build the Swift core against differential vectors generated from the Kotlin implementation with a seeded RNG, add a Kotlin-server-vs-Swift-client cross-handshake test in CI, and validate end-to-end on the macOS bench against a real pump before any iPhone work. Preserve the fixed 32-byte scalar encoding explicitly — variable-length encoding is a known source of a ~1.6% failure rate against the fixed 165/330-byte split offsets.

risks.risk: Bond loss cannot be repaired automatically. Every Android path that calls removeBond becomes a manual user procedure requiring both iOS Settings and physical access to the pump's pairing menu. An over-eager iOS failure classifier will strand users repeatedly.
risks.mitigation: Port the counter-based restraint faithfully (never invalidate after a successful session; tolerate 20 consecutive encryption failures), classify primarily on behavioral signals rather than error codes since CBError is coarser than Android's GATT statuses, and require hardware validation of every path that can reach the pairing-invalid state before release.

risks.risk: The pump accepts exactly one BLE connection at a time. On iOS this collides with t:connect, with the macOS bench, and with any watch-side experiment — and a user who has t:connect installed and connected will see this app simply never work, with no diagnostic distinguishing it from a broken pairing.
risks.mitigation: Rule out watch-side connection ownership architecturally, document the macOS bench and the iPhone as mutually exclusive, and detect the symptom pattern (connectable peripheral that never completes or immediately disconnects) to surface a specific 'another app or device is connected to your pump' message.

risks.risk: CBPeripheral.identifier replaces the MAC address as the pump's primary key. If it changes across a rebuild, reinstall, device restore or Bluetooth subsystem reset, the app loses its reconnect handle — and because the pump only advertises in pairing mode, recovery requires the user to physically re-enter pairing mode. This matters more here than in a normal app because fork-and-build users reinstall frequently and TestFlight builds expire every 90 days.
risks.mitigation: Store the pump serial from opcode 84 as a secondary fingerprint so a new identifier can be re-bound to the existing pump record, keep credentials in the Keychain (which survives app deletion), also probe retrieveConnectedPeripherals(withServices:) at launch, and validate identifier stability across a reinstall and a device restore on Daniel's hardware.

risks.risk: Keychain accessibility is a single decision that silently breaks background operation: with WhenUnlocked, the reconnect wake cannot read the pairing secret while the phone is locked and every background authentication fails, in a way that looks like a pump problem rather than a storage problem.
risks.mitigation: Use kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly, and add an explicit automated test plus a manual hardware check that a background reconnect authenticates successfully while the device is locked.

risks.risk: CoreBluetooth state restoration hands back peripherals with seconds of runtime and no application context. Attempting to resume a history pagination loop or a partial JPAKE handshake on restore will produce intermittent, hard-to-reproduce failures.
risks.mitigation: Treat every restored connection as a fresh session: re-authenticate from scratch (which matches Android's existing every-reconnect behavior), reset all assemblers and pending requests, and persist only a minimal durable resume record including the history cursor, which today lives only in memory on Android.

risks.risk: Swift traps on integer overflow where Kotlin wraps, and Data slices are not guaranteed aligned. The CRC loop, the 8-bit txId counter, the uint32 pump fields (the Mobi armSwVer 3628697757 exceeds Int32) and every little-endian load are all places where a literal translation crashes or silently misreads.
risks.mitigation: Use explicit overflow operators and explicit unsigned types throughout, load multi-byte values byte-by-byte rather than via unsafe pointer loads, and port every existing test vector before porting the corresponding implementation.

risks.risk: Semgrep's Kotlin and Java rulesets have no Swift equivalent, so the security posture of this module silently weakens if the CI workflow is copied by name rather than by intent.
risks.mitigation: Replace with CodeQL (language: swift) on a macOS runner for SAST, keep Semgrep p/secrets and OSV-Scanner unchanged (both work on Swift and on Package.resolved respectively), add SwiftLint, and state in the PRD that the compensating control for narrower generic rule coverage is the ported vector suite plus the cross-implementation crypto differential test.

risks.risk: Tandem Mobi is protocol-compatible but unverified on Android hardware, and no one on the iOS side has a Mobi at all. Shipping it as claimed parity means shipping an untested read path for a medical device, including the battery V2 path that only Mobi exercises.
risks.mitigation: Carry the Android verification status forward verbatim into the iOS app and its documentation (t:slim X2 verified, Mobi protocol-compatible/unverified), gate Mobi behind the same honest labeling, and treat any Mobi bug report as hardware-blocked until a maintainer with a Mobi appears.

risks.risk: Four readings — insulin on board, live basal, reservoir and battery — carry the read time rather than a pump timestamp, so a value cached by a failing poll is indistinguishable from a fresh one. On iOS, where poll gaps are routine and can be long, this is materially more dangerous than on Android.
risks.mitigation: Attach the acquisition time and an explicit freshness state to every reading at the driver boundary, and require the UI and the Watch to render age for these four values; do not carry Android's implicit-freshness model forward unchanged.

risks.risk: The live CGM read path validates against default 20–500 bounds rather than the user's configured SafetyLimits, and the live basal read applies no rate ceiling at all — a misframed 9-byte cargo can display an arbitrary basal rate. A literal port carries both defects into a new codebase.
risks.mitigation: Decide both deliberately and record the decision in the port; the low-risk resolution is to thread SafetyLimits through the live CGM path and apply the 15 000 mu/hr ceiling to the live basal parse, matching the history path, since both changes only tighten validation.

risks.risk: Status responses are matched by 8-bit txId alone with no opcode check, and the counter wraps every 256 requests. A late response from a wrapped transaction could satisfy a different pending request — for example completing an IoB read with basal bytes.
risks.mitigation: Keep the existing eviction of colliding pending entries and add a cheap opcode check (response opcode must equal request opcode + 1) at completion time; this is a strictly additive guard with no wire impact.

risks.risk: CoreBluetooth chooses notification versus indication from characteristic properties, whereas Android explicitly writes ENABLE_NOTIFICATION_VALUE. If any Tandem characteristic advertises both, iOS could subscribe differently than Android does.
risks.mitigation: Dump the properties of all six vendor characteristics during the first hardware session and confirm notify-only; if any advertises indicate as well, verify the pump's behavior under indications explicitly rather than assuming equivalence.

questions_for_pm: The live CGM read path validates glucose against the built-in 20–500 defaults instead of the user's configured SafetyLimits, while the history path uses the configured limits — the Android code notes this must be decided deliberately on any port. Should the iOS driver preserve the Android behavior exactly for bit-for-bit parity, or apply the user's configured limits on both paths (tightening validation, but making the two paths disagree with Android)?

Tandem Mobi is shipped on Android as 'protocol-compatible, unverified on hardware', and no one on the iOS side has a Mobi to test with — the maintainer with hardware has a t:slim X2. Should Mobi ship in the iOS app with the same unverified labeling, or be held out of the initial release until someone with the hardware can validate it?
